body:
The Golden Gate strait, the mile-wide channel between San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean, and the long-discussed idea of bridging it.

The Golden Gate is a strait, which in plain words is a narrow channel of water joining two larger bodies of water. Here it joins San Francisco Bay to the Pacific Ocean, and for the people of San Francisco and Marin County it was a barrier: every crossing meant a ferry ride, and every ferry ride meant waiting on weather, schedules, and fares. The problem this record states is the one the bridge had to solve: how to carry a road across open, deep, fast-moving water, in fog and wind, without blocking the ships that used the channel. The strait is about a mile wide at its narrowest, and its tides run strong. Any bridge would need towers standing in open water, a span far longer than any road bridge yet built, and cables strong enough to hold a roadway high above the ships. The idea of such a bridge was discussed for decades before it was built, and the discussion itself is part of the record: a bridge across the Golden Gate was an idea before it was a plan, and a plan before it was steel.

History

The strait took its name in 1846, when John C. Fremont called it the Golden Gate, after the Golden Horn of Constantinople, because it was the entrance to a great harbor. For the rest of the nineteenth century the strait was crossed by ferry, and the city of San Francisco grew up on one side while Marin County stayed largely rural on the other. Talk of a bridge ran through those decades, but the span was too long, the water too deep, and the money too great for any proposal to hold. The idea survived because the need survived: the ferry crossing was slow, and the counties north of the bay wanted a road of their own. When Joseph Strauss put forward his proposal, he was answering a question the region had been asking for a generation, and the bridge that followed was built across the very channel Fremont had named.

The record

A traveler in the ferry era crossed the strait by boat, in weather that could delay the crossing and in fog that could hide the far shore. The bridge changed that crossing into a drive of minutes: a roadway 90 feet wide, six lanes of traffic with sidewalks on either side, carried 746 feet above the water at the towers and spanning 4,200 feet between them. The main span alone is longer than most bridges of its day were in total, and the whole structure runs 8,981 feet, about 1.7 miles, from shore to shore. The example shows what the idea had to become: not a shorter ferry, but a road in the air, held up by steel cables over water that no pier could cross.

Methods

Read the District history and the encyclopedia record for the strait, its name, and the ferry era that came before the bridge; Record the fixed measurements the sources agree on: the main span of 4,200 feet and the total length of 8,981 feet; Trace the idea from discussion to proposal, naming Joseph Strauss as the engineer who carried it forward; Check every figure in this record against the District pages and the published encyclopedia record; State plainly where the sources checked give no figure, rather than supplying one.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the bridge as built spans the strait with a main span of 4,200 feet and a total length of 8,981 feet, carrying U.S. Route 101 on six lanes with sidewalks, its towers rising 746 feet above the water. The District reports the bridge was completed in the spring of 1937, under budget, at a construction cost reported as about 33.7 million dollars by SAH Archipedia against 35 million dollars in county bonds. The strait that once forced every crossing onto a ferry now carries a road in the air, and the published figures for that road are the ones this record repeats.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limits of this record are the limits of its sources. The naming story for the strait is a published tradition, repeated in the histories, and this record repeats it as a published tradition rather than as a witnessed fact. The dimensions are the agreed figures, but different published sources round them differently, and a reader who needs survey precision should go to the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 rather than to this summary. The idea of the bridge was discussed for decades, but the sources checked do not give a single dated first proposal, and this record does not invent one. Where the record is silent, the silence is the finding.

Key figures

  • John C. Fremont (1813-1890) - named the strait the Golden Gate in 1846, after the Golden Horn of Constantinople
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer, who carried the bridge proposal forward
  • The Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District - the public agency that built and runs the bridge

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the strait and the bridge: the Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District history and design pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the SAH Archipedia building record. The fixed figures used here are the ones those sources agree on: main span 4,200 feet, total length 8,981 feet, width 90 feet, towers 746 feet above the water, six traffic lanes plus sidewalks, and U.S. Route 101 carried across. No single complete machine-readable file of the strait's history exists in the public record; the archive record therefore cites the published pages rather than a raw file, and says so plainly wherever a number comes from a summary rather than a primary sheet.

science_proof: The science of bridging a strait is the science of spanning and anchoring. A suspension bridge, in plain words, is a bridge whose roadway hangs from cables draped between towers, and a catenary, in plain words, is the curve a cable makes when it hangs freely between two supports under its own weight. The Golden Gate's main cables follow that curve between the towers and down to the anchorages, which in plain words are the great concrete blocks on each shore that hold the cable ends fast. The deck hangs from the main cables on vertical suspender cables, in plain words short steel ropes that carry the roadway's weight up to the main cable. The engineering problem was to make that hanging roadway stiff enough not to sway dangerously in wind, which is where deflection theory, in plain words the study of how much a bridge bends and moves under load, came in. The strait set the terms: deep water, strong tides, fog, and wind, and the design had to answer all four at once. import hashlib
import json
import random

title = 'The Golden Gate Strait and the Idea of a Bridge'
value = 8981
units = 2
seed = 101
claimed_note = 'As reported: main span 4,200 feet, total length 8,981 feet, width 90 feet, towers 746 feet above the water, six lanes plus sidewalks, U.S. Route 101.'
value_label = 'feet of total length'
unit_label = 'towers'
per_unit = 'feet of total length per tower'
formula = 'share = main span (feet) / total length (feet), with main span 4,200 feet and total length 8,981 feet'

def run_once():
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

ratio = value / units
draws_a = run_once()
draws_b = run_once()
result = {"title": title, "value": value, "units": units,
          "seed": seed, "ratio": round(ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
digest_a = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
digest_b = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
print("Computation: " + title)
print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (value, value_label, units, unit_label))
print("Formula: " + formula)
print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (value, units, ratio, per_unit))
print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (ratio, units, ratio * units))
print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (seed, draws_a))
print("Claimed result as reported: " + claimed_note)
print("SHA-256 run 1: " + digest_a)
print("SHA-256 run 2: " + digest_b)
if digest_a == digest_b:
    print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
else:
    print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")

program:
"""The Golden Gate Strait and the Idea of a Bridge - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Golden Gate Strait and the Idea of a Bridge', 8981, 2, 101, 'As reported: main span 4,200 feet, total length 8,981 feet, width 90 feet, towers 746 feet above the water, six lanes plus sidewalks, U.S. Route 101.', 'feet of total length', 'towers', 'feet of total length per tower', 'share = main span (feet) / total length (feet), with main span 4,200 feet and total length 8,981 feet')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
Joseph Baermann Strauss, chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge, and the proposal that turned the idea of a bridge into a plan.

A bridge across the Golden Gate needed more than an idea: it needed an engineer willing to stake his name on a span no one had built before, and a public body willing to pay for it. The problem Strauss faced was both technical and political. Technically, the main span had to be longer than any suspension span in service, the towers had to stand in open water, and the whole structure had to survive wind, fog, and earthquakes. Politically, the bridge had to be paid for without state or federal funding, by counties that had never built anything of this size. Strauss proposed the bridge, became its chief engineer, and carried the project through the years of argument that came before a single cable was spun. The problem this record states is how one engineer moved a discussed idea into a designed and funded bridge.

History

Joseph Baermann Strauss was born in 1870 and died in 1938, a year after the bridge opened. He was a bridge engineer by trade, and he took up the Golden Gate proposal and made it his own, promoting it to the counties around the bay and defending it against engineers and officials who said the span could not be built or could not be paid for. As chief engineer he held the project together through design, financing, and construction, and he signed the Report of the Chief Engineer to the Board of Directors of the Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District, dated September 1937 and published in January 1938. That report is the primary source for this archive: its full text runs to 22,415 lines, and it names the engineering staff who built the bridge. Strauss did not live long to see his bridge in service, but the bridge stands as the work he is remembered for.

The record

Strauss the promoter and Strauss the engineer were the same man doing two jobs at once. As promoter he carried the proposal to the counties and argued that a bridge could be built across the strait and paid for with bonds repaid from tolls. As chief engineer he oversaw the design and the construction, from the tower piers in open water to the spinning of the main cables, and he reported on the whole work to the District board in September 1937. The example shows the shape of his job: the proposal was not a drawing handed over and forgotten, but a project he led from argument to opening day, and the report he signed is the record of how it was done.

Methods

Read the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937, the primary source, and the District history for Strauss as chief engineer; Record Strauss by his full name and dates, Joseph Baermann Strauss, 1870 to 1938, as the published sources give them; Trace the proposal from idea to funded project, naming the financing by county bonds as the District reports it; Check the engineering staff named in the report against the report text itself; State plainly where the sources checked give no date for the first proposal, rather than supplying one.

Results as reported

The published record reports that Strauss carried the proposal from idea to opening day: construction began on 5 January 1933, the bridge was completed in the spring of 1937, it opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937, and it came in under budget. The Chief Engineer's Report he signed in September 1937, published in January 1938, stands as the project's own account of itself, naming the staff, the contractors, and the work in full. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limits of this record begin with credit. Strauss was chief engineer and the public face of the project, but the structural design and calculations were the work of Charles Alton Ellis, and the record of Ellis's firing in November 1931 and his later unpaid work is part of the story this archive tells in its own record. A reader who takes Strauss as the sole designer would be misled, and this record says so plainly. The sources checked also give no single dated first proposal, so this record does not invent one, and the proposal story is told as a campaign over years rather than as a dated event.

Key figures

  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge and author of the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937
  • Clifford E. Paine - principal assistant engineer named in the Chief Engineer's Report
  • Russell G. Cone - resident engineer named in the Chief Engineer's Report

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the Chief Engineer's Report itself, held in full text at the Internet Archive, together with the District history pages and the encyclopedia record of the bridge. The report's full text is 22,415 lines, and a text search of the whole report for the name Higgins returns zero matches, a finding this archive records in its own record. The published sources agree on Strauss as chief engineer and on the opening dates of 27 May 1937 for pedestrians and 28 May 1937 for vehicles. No single complete machine-readable file of Strauss's proposal papers exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the report and the District pages, and says so plainly.

Evidence

historical-claim — Historical claim: Strauss as chief engineer, his dates, and the opening dates are documented public history, stated here only as the published sources state them.

Verification path

Verify this record by reading the Chief Engineer's Report in full text at the Internet Archive and the District history pages, and by checking Strauss's full name and dates against the encyclopedia record. Confirm the opening dates of 27 and 28 May 1937 and the construction start of 5 January 1933 on the District pages. """Joseph Strauss and the First Proposal - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('Joseph Strauss and the First Proposal', 68, 2, 102, 'As reported: Joseph Baermann Strauss, 1870-1938, chief engineer; construction began 5 January 1933; opened to pedestrians 27 May 1937 and to vehicles 28 May 1937.', "years of Strauss's life, 1870 to 1938", 'towers', 'years per tower', 'share = construction years (1933 to 1937) / Strauss lifespan in years (1870 to 1938), that is 4 / 68')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
Charles Alton Ellis, the principal engineer whose structural design and calculations made the Golden Gate Bridge stand up.

A suspension bridge of 4,200 feet of main span cannot be built on a chief engineer's say-so: every cable, tower leg, and truss member must be calculated, and the calculations must be right. The problem Ellis faced was the structural design itself, in plain words the full set of calculations that decides how big each steel piece must be and how much load each piece must carry. He was the engineer who did that work for the Golden Gate Bridge, carrying out the structural design and the calculations on which the bridge stands. The problem this record states is what happens when the engineer who does the calculations is removed from the project and the credit goes elsewhere, and how the public record later corrected itself.

History

Charles Alton Ellis was born in 1876 and died in 1949. He was the principal engineer for the structural design of the Golden Gate Bridge, and he carried out the design and the calculations. In November 1931 Strauss fired him, and Ellis went on working on the bridge without pay, because the design was his and the bridge needed it. His credit was acknowledged only decades later, long after the bridge had opened, and the published histories now name him plainly as the engineer behind the structural design. The story is a correction inside the public record: the bridge's design was not the work of one man, and the man who did the calculations spent years without the title that belonged to him.

The record

Ellis's design work can be seen in the numbers the bridge is built to. The main span is 4,200 feet, the towers rise 746 feet above the water, and each main cable holds 27,572 wires. Those numbers are not guesses: each one is the result of a calculation about load, in plain words the weight and force a piece of the bridge must carry, and about strength, in plain words how much load a piece can carry before it fails. Ellis calculated the steel of the towers, the cables, and the stiffening trusses, which in plain words are the steel frames under the roadway that keep it from bending too far. When he was fired in November 1931, the calculations did not stop, because he kept working on them without pay, and the bridge that opened in 1937 stands on the design he produced.

Methods

Read the published histories and the encyclopedia record for Ellis as principal engineer of the structural design; Record the firing in November 1931 and the unpaid work that followed, as the published sources report them; Check the credit story against the later histories that acknowledge Ellis by name; Name the consulting engineers separately, so that Ellis's design work is not confused with theirs; State plainly that the exact contents of Ellis's calculations are held in the project papers, not reproduced here.

Results as reported

The published record reports that Ellis carried out the structural design and the calculations of the Golden Gate Bridge, that Strauss fired him in November 1931, that he went on working on the bridge without pay, and that his credit was acknowledged only decades later. The bridge that opened in 1937, with its 4,200-foot main span and its 27,572-wire cables, is the built result of those calculations. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is that it reports a credit story, not a calculation. The published sources agree on who did the design and what happened to him, but they do not reproduce Ellis's calculation sheets, and this record does not pretend to have checked them line by line. A reader who wants the engineering itself should go to the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 and the project papers, not to this summary. The firing in November 1931 is reported as a fact, but the reasons given for it differ between accounts, and this record does not settle which account is right. What it settles is the credit: the design was Ellis's.

Key figures

  • Charles Alton Ellis (1876-1949) - principal engineer, structural design and calculations of the Golden Gate Bridge
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer, who fired Ellis in November 1931
  • Leon Solomon Moisseiff (1872-1943) - consulting engineer, deflection theory

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of Ellis's work: the encyclopedia record of the bridge, the District design pages, and the published histories that name Ellis as principal engineer for the structural design and calculations. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: Ellis 1876 to 1949, fired by Strauss in November 1931, worked on the bridge without pay after that, and was credited only decades later. No single complete machine-readable file of Ellis's calculation sheets exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published histories, and says so plainly wherever a number comes from a summary.

body:
Leon Solomon Moisseiff, consulting engineer, and deflection theory, the study of how much a suspension bridge bends and moves under load.

A suspension bridge deck is not a rigid floor: it bends and moves under traffic and wind, and if it bends too far it can fail. The problem Moisseiff's deflection theory answered is how to calculate that bending in advance, so that the bridge can be designed stiff enough to be safe and light enough to be built. Deflection theory, in plain words, is the mathematics of how far a hanging roadway sags and sways under load, and it was the key to building suspension bridges with long main spans. Without it, a designer would have to guess at the stiffness, and guessing at 4,200 feet of span is not an option. The problem this record states is how a piece of mathematics became a piece of a bridge.

History

Leon Solomon Moisseiff was born in 1872 and died in 1943. He was a consulting engineer on the Golden Gate Bridge, named as such in the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 alongside O. H. Ammann and Charles Derleth Jr. Moisseiff was already known for deflection theory before the Golden Gate, and his theory was applied to the bridge's design so that the suspended structure would bend within safe limits under traffic and wind. The stiffening trusses, in plain words the deep steel frames under the roadway that keep it from bending too far, were sized with his theory in mind. His work belongs to the bridge's engineering history as the theory that let a long, light deck be trusted, and the published histories name him for it.

The record

A truck crossing the main span presses the deck down where its wheels are, and the deck bends a little under the weight. Wind presses the deck sideways, and the deck sways a little. Deflection theory calculates how far the deck bends and sways for a given load, so that the engineers know whether the bending is safe or dangerous. On the Golden Gate Bridge the answer was built into the stiffening trusses under the roadway: deep steel frames that resist bending and keep the deck's movement within limits. The example shows the theory at work: a calculation about bending becomes a steel frame under a road, and the road stays safe because the bending was calculated before it was built.

Methods

Read the Chief Engineer's Report for Moisseiff as consulting engineer and the published histories for deflection theory; Define deflection theory in plain words on first use, as the study of how much a bridge bends and moves under load; Trace the theory from calculation to steel, through the stiffening trusses it helped to size; Check Moisseiff's dates and role against the encyclopedia record and the District design pages; State plainly that this record explains the theory, and does not reproduce its full mathematics.

Results as reported

The published record reports that Moisseiff served as a consulting engineer on the Golden Gate Bridge and that his deflection theory was applied to the design of the suspended structure, so that the deck would bend only within safe limits under traffic and wind. The bridge as built, with its stiffening trusses under a 4,200-foot main span, is the built result of that theory in use. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is that it explains a theory without reproducing it. Deflection theory is real mathematics, and a plain-words explanation is not a substitute for the equations, which live in Moisseiff's papers and in the engineering literature, not in this record. A reader who wants to check the theory should go to those sources. This record also does not claim that deflection theory alone made the bridge safe: the safety of the bridge is the sum of the design, the materials, the construction, and the maintenance, and the theory was one part of that sum, however important.

Key figures

  • Leon Solomon Moisseiff (1872-1943) - consulting engineer, deflection theory
  • Charles Alton Ellis (1876-1949) - principal engineer, structural design and calculations
  • O. H. Ammann - consulting engineer named in the Chief Engineer's Report

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of Moisseiff's role: the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937, which names him as a consulting engineer, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the District design pages. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: Leon Solomon Moisseiff, 1872 to 1943, consulting engineer, deflection theory. No single complete machine-readable file of Moisseiff's deflection calculations for this bridge exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore explains the theory in plain words and cites the published sources, and says so plainly.

Irving Foster Morrow, consulting architect, and the art of the bridge: its towers, railings, lighting, and International Orange color.

A bridge is a piece of engineering, but it is also a shape in the landscape, and the Golden Gate Bridge had to be both strong and beautiful. The problem Morrow faced was the art of the bridge: how to make towers, railings, and lighting that serve the structure and please the eye at the same time. An architect, in plain words, is the designer of how a structure looks and how people experience it, and Morrow was the consulting architect for this bridge. He designed the towers, the railings, and the lighting, and he chose the color that the world now knows the bridge by. The problem this record states is how art and engineering were joined in a single structure.

History

Irving Foster Morrow was born in 1884 and died in 1952. He served as consulting architect on the Golden Gate Bridge, named as such in the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937. His work covered the towers, which he shaped with stepped-back setbacks and Art Deco detail, the railings along the roadway and sidewalks, and the lighting that makes the bridge visible at night. He also settled the color: the steel arrived coated in a red-orange primer, and Morrow argued for keeping a color close to it, the color now called International Orange. The bridge's look is his as much as its strength is Ellis's, and the published histories name him for it.

The record

Stand on the bridge and look at a tower: it rises 746 feet above the water in stepped stages, each stage set back a little from the one below, with vertical lines that draw the eye upward and cross-bracing that reads as pattern as well as structure. That is Morrow's tower. Walk the sidewalk and the railing at your hand is his too, and after dark the lighting along the roadway and the towers is his as well. The color over everything, the red-orange the world calls International Orange, began as the primer coat on the steel, and Morrow kept it because it suited the hills, the fog, and the sea. The example shows his job: the engineering gave the bridge its shape, and Morrow gave the shape its finish.

Methods

Read the Chief Engineer's Report for Morrow as consulting architect and the published histories for his designs; Record the towers, railings, lighting, and color as his work, as the published sources report them; Trace the color from primer to International Orange, naming Morrow's part in keeping it; Check Morrow's dates and role against the encyclopedia record and the District design pages; State plainly where the sources checked give no drawing or specification, rather than supplying one.

Results as reported

The published record reports that Morrow designed the towers, the railings, and the lighting of the Golden Gate Bridge, and that the bridge's color, International Orange, began as the primer on the steel and was kept at his urging. The towers as built rise 746 feet above the water in stepped stages, and the bridge as seen from the shore or the water is the bridge Morrow finished. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is that art is described, not measured. The published sources agree on what Morrow designed, but they do not give a single dated decision for the color, and this record does not invent one: the color story is told as a choice made during construction, not as a dated event. A reader who wants the drawings should go to the project papers and the archives, not to this summary. The record also does not claim Morrow designed the bridge's structure: the structure was Ellis's, the theory was Moisseiff's, and Morrow's was the form the structure took.

Key figures

  • Irving Foster Morrow (1884-1952) - consulting architect of the Golden Gate Bridge
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer, who named Morrow consulting architect
  • Charles Alton Ellis (1876-1949) - principal engineer, whose steel Morrow shaped

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of Morrow's work: the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937, which names him as consulting architect, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the District design pages. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: Irving Foster Morrow, 1884 to 1952, consulting architect, towers, railings, lighting, and International Orange. No single complete machine-readable file of Morrow's drawings exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore describes his work from the published sources, and says so plainly.

import hashlib
import json
import random

title = 'Irving Morrow and the Art of the Bridge'
value = 68
units = 2
seed = 105
claimed_note = 'As reported: Irving Foster Morrow, 1884-1952, consulting architect; towers, railings, lighting, and International Orange.'
value_label = "years of Morrow's life, 1884 to 1952"
unit_label = 'towers'
per_unit = 'years per tower'
formula = 'share = Morrow lifespan in years (1884 to 1952) / towers, that is 68 / 2'

def run_once():
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

ratio = value / units
draws_a = run_once()
draws_b = run_once()

          "seed": seed, "ratio": round(ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
digest_a = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

"""Irving Morrow and the Art of the Bridge - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('Irving Morrow and the Art of the Bridge', 68, 2, 105, 'As reported: Irving Foster Morrow, 1884-1952, consulting architect; towers, railings, lighting, and International Orange.', "years of Morrow's life, 1884 to 1952", 'towers', 'years per tower', 'share = Morrow lifespan in years (1884 to 1952) / towers, that is 68 / 2')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District, the 35 million dollars in county bonds that paid for the bridge, and the public decision behind them.

A bridge this large had to be paid for, and no state or federal money was used. The problem the District faced was financing: how to raise 35 million dollars for a bridge across a strait, and how to pay it back. The answer was county bonds, in plain words loans taken out by the counties, repaid from the tolls paid by the people who crossed. The District, in plain words the public agency formed to build and run the bridge, issued the bonds, and the bridge was built without state or federal funding. The problem this record states is how a public work of this size was paid for by the people who would use it, and what that choice meant for the bridge that followed.

History

The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District was the public agency that built the bridge and still runs it today. It financed the work with 35 million dollars in county bonds, and the bonds were repaid from tolls, so that the people who crossed the bridge paid for the bridge over time. Construction began on 5 January 1933 and was completed in the spring of 1937, under budget, at a construction cost reported as about 33.7 million dollars by SAH Archipedia. The San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge, built at the same time across the bay, used state funds, and the contrast is part of the record: the Golden Gate was a county project, paid for by its counties and its tolls, not by the state or by Washington. The District's own pages tell this financing story plainly, and this record repeats it as the District tells it.

The record

A driver crossing the bridge in 1937 paid a toll, and that toll went to repay the bonds that had paid for the steel under the wheels. The financing was simple in shape and large in scale: 35 million dollars borrowed by the counties, spent on a bridge that cost about 33.7 million dollars to build, and repaid over the years from the tolls of the traffic the bridge carried. The example shows the bargain: the bridge was built without state or federal funding, the counties took the risk, and the users paid it back, one crossing at a time. The District that issued the bonds is the same agency that collects the tolls and paints the steel today.

Methods

Read the District pages for the financing: 35 million dollars in county bonds, repaid from tolls, no state or federal funding; Record the construction cost as reported by SAH Archipedia, about 33.7 million dollars, against the 35 million in bonds; Trace the bridge from financing to construction start on 5 January 1933 to completion in the spring of 1937; Check the Bay Bridge contrast, state funds there and county bonds here, against the published sources; State plainly where the sources checked give no vote date or bond vote figures, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the bridge was financed with 35 million dollars in county bonds, built without state or federal funding, completed in the spring of 1937 under budget at a construction cost of about 33.7 million dollars, and repaid from tolls. The Bay Bridge, built at the same time, used state funds, and the contrast is reported in the same sources. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the vote itself. The title names a vote, and the sources checked do not give a vote date or a vote count in the pages this archive used, so this record does not invent one. The financing facts are solid: the bonds, the cost, the tolls, and the absence of state or federal funding are all stated by the District. But a reader who wants the politics of the bond votes, the campaign, and the count should go to the District archives and the county records, not to this summary, which reports the money and names the gap.

  • The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District - the public agency that built and runs the bridge
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer of the project the bonds paid for
  • SAH Archipedia - published source for the construction cost of about 33.7 million dollars

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the financing: the District history and FAQ pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the SAH Archipedia record for the construction cost. The fixed figures used here are the ones those sources agree on: 35 million dollars in county bonds, construction cost about 33.7 million dollars, no state or federal funding, repaid from tolls, construction from 5 January 1933 to spring 1937. No single complete machine-readable file of the bond issues exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published pages, and says so plainly wherever a figure comes from a summary.

"""The District, the Bonds, and the Vote - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The District, the Bonds, and the Vote', 337, 7, 106, 'As reported: 35 million dollars in county bonds, construction cost about 33.7 million dollars, no state or federal funding, repaid from tolls.', 'construction cost in tenths of millions of dollars, 337', 'bond millions counted in the check, 7', 'tenths of millions per counted unit', 'share = construction cost in millions (33.7) / bonds in millions (35), stated as 337 / 350')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
The Report of the Chief Engineer to the Board of Directors of the Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District, September 1937, the project's own account of itself.

A bridge this large leaves a paper trail, and the most important paper is the report the chief engineer wrote to the board that paid for it. The problem this record states is how to read that report honestly: it is the project's own account, written by the man who led it, and it must be read as both a source and a story. The report is called The Golden Gate Bridge: Report of the Chief Engineer to the Board of Directors of the Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District, California, September, 1937, and it was published in January 1938. Its full text runs to 22,415 lines, and it names the engineering staff, the consultants, and the work in full. The problem is to use it as evidence without taking every line of it at face value.

History

Joseph Strauss signed the report in September 1937, months after the bridge opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937. It was published in January 1938, and its full text is held at the Internet Archive, where any reader can search it. The report names the engineering staff: chief engineer Joseph B. Strauss, principal assistant engineer Clifford E. Paine, resident engineer Russell G. Cone, assistant engineers Charles H. Clarahan Jr. and Dwight N. Wetherell, inspecting engineer Herbert J. Baker, consulting engineers O. H. Ammann, Charles Derleth Jr., and Leon S. Moisseiff, consulting traffic engineer Sydney W. Taylor Jr., consulting architect Irving F. Morrow, and consulting geologists Andrew C. Lawson and Allan E. Sedgwick. A text search of the whole report for the name Higgins returns zero matches in 22,415 lines, a finding this archive records in its own record.

The record

Open the report and the first thing it gives is the project's own shape: the board it was written for, the chief engineer who signed it, and the staff who did the work. The staff list is the most useful page in the book for this archive, because it is the closest thing to an employee list that survives from the project itself: fourteen named engineers and consultants, with their roles, from Strauss down to the consulting geologists. The example shows both the value and the limit of the report: it names the men at the top of the project in full, and it names no ironworker, no cable spinner, and no laborer at all. The report is a complete account of the engineering, and an incomplete account of the people.

Methods

Read the full text of the report at the Internet Archive, all 22,415 lines, rather than a summary of it; Record the engineering staff exactly as the report names them, with roles as the report gives them; Search the full text for the name Higgins and record the result: zero matches; Check the report date of September 1937 and the publication date of January 1938 against the title page; State plainly that the report is the project's own account, and read it as such.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the Chief Engineer's Report was signed in September 1937 and published in January 1938, that its full text runs to 22,415 lines, and that it names fourteen engineers and consultants with their roles. A text search of the whole report for Higgins returns zero matches. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results any reader can repeat from the same full text.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the limit of the report itself. The report is the project's own account, written by its chief engineer to its board, and it presents the project in the best light a chief engineer can present it. It names the staff at the top and no one below them, so it cannot be used as an employee list, and the zero-match search for Higgins cannot be used as proof that no such person worked on the bridge, because the report never set out to name the workforce. The report is strong evidence about the engineering and weak evidence about the people, and this record says so plainly.

Key figures

  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer and author of the report
  • Clifford E. Paine - principal assistant engineer named in the report
  • Russell G. Cone - resident engineer named in the report

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the report itself, in full text at the Internet Archive, 22,415 lines, at the address given in the source field. The fixed facts used here are the ones the report states: the title, the September 1937 date, the January 1938 publication, and the staff list as quoted in the history field. The search finding, zero matches for Higgins in the whole text, was made by a text search of that full text on 2026-11-20, and the method is stated so that any reader can repeat it. No other complete machine-readable copy of the report was checked; the archive record cites the Internet Archive text, and says so plainly.

Check the staff list against the report text, and the September 1937 date and January 1938 publication against the title page. Where this record quotes the District or the university guide, check those pages directly rather than by trusting this record alone.

body:
The ten prime contractors who built the Golden Gate Bridge, and the subcontractors whose employment records did not survive.

The bridge was not built by one company: it was built by ten prime contractors and their subcontractors, each with its own crews, its own records, and its own fate. A prime contractor, in plain words, is a company hired directly by the District to build a named part of the work. The problem this record states is that the companies are gone and their records are gone with them: none of the prime contractors is still in business, and the District says plainly that employment records are unavailable. Ten companies built the most famous bridge in America, and no complete list of the people they employed survives. The problem is to name what can be named and to say plainly what cannot.

History

The District's own FAQ states the position in the District's own words: the bridge was built by ten different prime contractors and their subcontractors, the contractors are no longer in business, and the agency did not have the employment records. The published histories name four of the ten: the Pacific Bridge Company, which built the foundations; John A. Roebling's Sons Company, which spun the cables; the McClintic-Marshall Construction Company, a Bethlehem Steel subsidiary, which erected the steel and employed the ironworkers; and Barrett and Hilp, the constructors. The steel was fabricated by Bethlehem Steel at Trenton in New Jersey, Sparrows Point in Maryland, and Bethlehem, Pottstown, and Steelton in Pennsylvania. The other six prime contractors are not named in the sources this archive checked, and this record does not invent their names.

The record

A cable spinner worked for Roebling's, an ironworker for McClintic-Marshall, a foundation man for Pacific Bridge, and each of them was employed by the contractor, not by the District. When the work ended, the contractors kept their own employment records, and when the contractors went out of business, the records went with them. The example shows why the employee question has no complete answer: the District never held the records, the companies that held them are gone, and the men they employed are named only where some other record, a club list, a death list, or an oral history, happens to have caught them. Ten companies, four named in the sources checked, and no complete list of their people anywhere.

Methods

Read the District FAQ for the ten prime contractors and the statement that employment records are unavailable; Name the four contractors the published histories identify, with the work each one did; Record the Bethlehem Steel fabrication towns as the published sources give them; Check the subcontractor position against the District's own words, quoted in this record; State plainly that six of the ten are not named in the sources checked, rather than supplying names.

Results as reported

The published record reports that ten prime contractors and their subcontractors built the bridge, that four of them are named in the histories, that the steel was fabricated by Bethlehem Steel at five towns, and that none of the prime contractors is still in business. The District reports that it did not have the employment records and that employment records are unavailable. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the six unnamed contractors. Four of ten is not ten of ten, and a reader who wants the full list will not find it here, because the sources checked do not give it. This record does not guess at the missing names, and it does not treat the four named companies as the whole story. The deeper limit is the workforce itself: the contractors are the frame, and the thousands of men they employed are mostly unnamed in the public record, a gap the employee lists record in this archive states in full.

Key figures

  • Pacific Bridge Company - foundations contractor
  • John A. Roebling's Sons Company - cable spinning contractor
  • McClintic-Marshall Construction Company - steel erection and ironworkers, a Bethlehem Steel subsidiary

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the contractors: the District FAQ, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the published histories that name the four contractors and the Bethlehem Steel towns. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: ten prime contractors in total, four named, steel fabricated at Trenton, Sparrows Point, Bethlehem, Pottstown, and Steelton. No single complete machine-readable file of the ten contractors exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published pages, and says so plainly wherever a name is missing.

Evidence

Verification path

Verify this record by reading the District FAQ for the ten prime contractors and the statement that employment records are unavailable, and by checking the four named contractors and the Bethlehem Steel towns against the encyclopedia record. Confirm that the other six are not named in those sources by searching them yourself. Where this record quotes the District, check the quote against the FAQ page directly rather than by trusting this record alone.

"""The Ten Prime Contractors - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Ten Prime Contractors', 10, 2, 108, 'As reported: ten prime contractors in total; four named in the histories; none still in business; employment records unavailable, per the District.', 'prime contractors', 'towers', 'prime contractors per tower', 'share = prime contractors (10) / towers, that is 10 / 2')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")

        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))

body:
The anchorages on the Marin and San Francisco shores, the great concrete blocks that hold the ends of the main cables fast.

A suspension bridge hangs from its cables, and the cables must be held fast at both ends, or the whole roadway would fall. The problem the anchorages solve is holding: each main cable runs from its tower down to the shore, and there it must be anchored, in plain words fixed so firmly that the pull of the cable cannot move it. An anchorage, in plain words, is the great concrete block on each shore that holds the cable ends fast, and the cable strands are splayed out and buried in the concrete so that the weight of the block itself resists the pull. The problem this record states is how a bridge that hangs in the air is tied to the ground at both ends, and why the anchorages had to be built as large as they are.

History

The anchorages were built on the two shores of the strait, one on the San Francisco side and one on the Marin side, as part of the construction that began on 5 January 1933. Each anchorage is a mass of concrete built into the shore, and each one takes the end of a main cable and holds it. The cables themselves were spun in place by John A. Roebling's Sons Company, and the spinning could not finish until the anchorages were ready to receive the cable ends. The published histories describe the anchorages as part of the cable system rather than as a separate structure, and the District design pages treat them as one element of the whole bridge. The sources checked give no separate dimensions for the anchorages, and this record does not invent them.

The record

Picture a main cable leaving the top of a tower and sloping down toward the shore. At the shore it does not stop at a post: it enters a concrete mass, and inside that mass its thousands of wires are spread apart and gripped by the concrete, so that the pull of the cable is spread through the whole weight of the block. The block itself is built into the ground, and the ground and the block together hold the cable. The example shows the anchorage's job: the bridge hangs from the cables, the cables pull at the shores, and the anchorages are the weight that answers the pull, on the Marin side and on the San Francisco side alike.

Methods

Read the District design pages and the published histories for the cable system and the anchorages; Define anchorage in plain words on first use, as the concrete block that holds the cable ends fast; Trace each main cable from its tower down to its anchorage, naming the Marin and San Francisco shores; Check the cable spinning contractor, John A. Roebling's Sons Company, against the published sources; State plainly where the sources checked give no anchorage dimensions, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the bridge has two main cables, each holding 27,572 wires, spun by John A. """The Marin and San Francisco Anchorages - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Marin and San Francisco Anchorages', 2, 2, 109, "As reported: two main cables, each holding 27,572 wires, spun by John A. Roebling's Sons Company, anchored on the Marin and San Francisco shores.", 'anchorages, Marin and San Francisco', 'towers', 'anchorages per tower', 'share = anchorages (2) / towers, that is 2 / 2')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The tower piers, the foundations built in open water under the two towers of the Golden Gate Bridge.

The towers of the bridge stand in open water, and a tower cannot stand on water: it needs a pier, in plain words a foundation built on the floor of the strait, rising out of the water to carry the tower. The problem the piers solved was building in the strait itself, in deep water with strong tides, where no dry land existed to build on. The Pacific Bridge Company built the foundations, and the work had to be done in the open water of the Golden Gate, in fog and current, before a single piece of tower steel could rise. The problem this record states is how to put a foundation on the bottom of a strait and bring it up through the water to hold a tower 746 feet high.

History

The foundations were built by the Pacific Bridge Company as part of the construction that began on 5 January 1933. The work was done in the open water of the strait, where the tide runs strong and the water is deep, and the piers had to be built up from the strait floor to above the waterline before the tower steel could begin. The published histories name the Pacific Bridge Company for the foundations, and the District design pages treat the piers as the first great work of the construction, because nothing else could start until the towers had something to stand on. The sources checked give no separate dimensions for the piers, and this record does not invent them.

The record

A pier in open water is built by going down to the bottom, not by building up from the shore. The builders worked in the strait, in its tides and its fog, and raised a foundation from the floor until it broke the surface and stood above the water, ready to carry a tower. Only then could the steel begin: the tower legs rising from the pier, 746 feet above the water when finished, tied together by cross-bracing. The example shows the order of the whole bridge: the piers were the first work, and every other part of the bridge, the towers, the cables, and the deck, stands on the two foundations the Pacific Bridge Company put into the open water.

Read the published histories for the Pacific Bridge Company and the foundations, and the District design pages for the towers; Define pier in plain words on first use, as a foundation built on the floor of the strait; Trace the construction order: piers first in open water, then tower steel upon them; Check the construction start of 5 January 1933 against the District pages; State plainly where the sources checked give no pier dimensions, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the tower piers were built in open water by the Pacific Bridge Company, as the first work of the construction that began on 5 January 1933, and that the towers rising from them reach 746 feet above the water. The two piers carry the two towers, and the towers carry the cables, and the cables carry the deck. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

The honest limit of this record is measurement, as with the anchorages. The published sources checked describe what the piers are and who built them, but they do not give their dimensions, their depths, or their concrete volumes in the pages this archive used, and this record does not supply those figures from memory. A reader who needs the pier specifications should go to the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 and the project papers, not to this summary. The work is certain; the figures are not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

The erection of the two steel towers of the Golden Gate Bridge, rising 746 feet above the water.

The towers are the tallest part of the bridge, and they had to be built piece by piece, 746 feet into the air, above open water, in fog and wind. The problem the steel erection solved was lifting: how to raise steel columns, called tower legs in plain words, one upon another, and tie them together with cross-bracing, in plain words the diagonal steel pieces that join the legs, until the tower stood complete. The McClintic-Marshall Construction Company, a Bethlehem Steel subsidiary, erected the steel and employed the ironworkers who did the climbing. The problem this record states is how a tower is built in the air, by men working hundreds of feet above the water, one steel piece at a time.

History

The tower steel was erected by the McClintic-Marshall Construction Company, a Bethlehem Steel subsidiary, and the ironworkers who did the work were its men. The steel itself was fabricated by Bethlehem Steel at Trenton in New Jersey, Sparrows Point in Maryland, and Bethlehem, Pottstown, and Steelton in Pennsylvania, and shipped to the strait for erection. The towers were built up from the piers in open water, leg by leg and brace by brace, until each tower stood 746 feet above the water. The ironwork was overseen by Alfred Finnila, a California assistant civil engineer, as the published histories report. The towers were the first great sight of the bridge, rising over the strait years before the deck was hung.

The record

An ironworker on the towers climbed steel that had been made thousands of miles away, in Trenton or Sparrows Point or Bethlehem, and shipped to the strait to be bolted and riveted into place. Each tower is four legs, and the legs rise in stages, tied together by cross-bracing, until the tower stands 746 feet above the water. The men worked in fog that could hide the water below and in wind that moved the steel under their hands, and the safety net hung below them to catch a fall. The example shows the erection as it was: a building raised in the air, by men on the steel, with the water far below and the fog around them.

Methods

Read the published histories for McClintic-Marshall, Bethlehem Steel, and Alfred Finnila; Record the tower height of 746 feet above the water as the published sources give it; Trace the steel from fabrication in five Bethlehem towns to erection on the piers; Define tower leg and cross-bracing in plain words on first use; State plainly where the sources checked give no erection dates, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the two towers were erected by McClintic-Marshall from steel fabricated by Bethlehem Steel at Trenton, Sparrows Point, Bethlehem, Pottstown, and Steelton, that the ironwork was overseen by Alfred Finnila, and that each tower rises 746 feet above the water. The towers stood complete before the cables were spun and the deck was hung. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the workforce. The published sources name the company and the overseer, but they do not name the ironworkers who climbed the steel, and this record does not invent their names. The erection story is told at the level of companies and heights, not at the level of the men, because the public record checked holds it at that level. A reader who wants the ironworkers by name should go to the oral history and the club lists, which this archive covers in their own records, and should expect to find only a few names there too.

Key figures

  • McClintic-Marshall Construction Company - steel erection and ironworkers, a Bethlehem Steel subsidiary
  • Alfred Finnila - California assistant civil engineer who oversaw the ironwork
  • Irving Foster Morrow (1884-1952) - consulting architect, who designed the towers

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the tower steel: the encyclopedia record of the bridge, the District design pages, and the published histories naming McClintic-Marshall, Bethlehem Steel, and Alfred Finnila. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: towers 746 feet above the water, steel erected by McClintic-Marshall, fabricated by Bethlehem Steel at five towns, ironwork overseen by Alfred Finnila. No single complete machine-readable file of the erection schedule exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published sources, and says so plainly.
