The two main cables of the Golden Gate Bridge, each spun in place from 27,572 steel wires by John A. Roebling's Sons Company.

A suspension bridge hangs from its main cables, and the main cables of this bridge had to be stronger than any cables yet made. The problem the cable spinning solved was making them: a main cable cannot be bought in a length of 8,981 feet and lifted into place, so it must be spun in place, in plain words built wire by wire, by carrying single wires back and forth across the span until the cable is complete. John A. Roebling's Sons Company spun the cables, and each cable holds 27,572 wires. The problem this record states is how 27,572 separate wires become one cable strong enough to hold a roadway in the air.

History

The cables were spun by John A. Roebling's Sons Company, the cable spinning contractor, as part of the construction that began on 5 January 1933. Spinning means carrying one wire at a time across the span, from anchorage to anchorage over the towers, and laying it beside the wires before it, again and again, until the bundle is complete. Each main cable holds 27,572 wires, and the two cables together hold 55,144 wires. The wires were then squeezed together into a round cable and wrapped, so that the bundle acts as one piece of steel. The published histories name Roebling's for the spinning, and the District design pages treat the cables as the heart of the bridge, because everything else hangs from them.

The record

A spinning wheel carries a single wire across the span, from the Marin anchorage over the towers to the San Francisco anchorage, and lays it in place. Then it goes back, and lays another wire beside the first, and another, and another, until 27,572 wires lie side by side in one cable. The example shows the scale of the work: a cable is not a rope bought in a shop, but a bundle built one wire at a time, across a mile of open water, in the fog and the wind of the strait. When the spinning was done, the wires were squeezed into a round cable and wrapped, and the roadway could be hung from them.

Methods

Read the published histories and the District design pages for Roebling's cable spinning; Record the wire count of 27,572 per cable as the published sources give it; Define spinning in plain words on first use, as building a cable wire by wire across the span; Trace each cable from anchorage to anchorage over the two towers; Check the total of 55,144 wires for both cables by adding the two cable counts.

Results as reported

The published record reports that each main cable holds 27,572 wires, that the two cables together hold 55,144 wires, and that the cables were spun in place by John A. Roebling's Sons Company. The cables carry the roadway through the suspender cables, and the bridge hangs from them. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the wire itself. The published sources agree on the count of 27,572 wires per cable, but they do not give the wire diameter, the wire strength, or the spinning schedule in the pages this archive used, and this record does not supply those figures from memory. A reader who needs the cable specifications should go to the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 and the project papers, not to this summary. The count is certain; the specifications are not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

  • John A. Roebling's Sons Company - cable spinning contractor
  • Charles Alton Ellis (1876-1949) - principal engineer, structural design and calculations
  • Leon Solomon Moisseiff (1872-1943) - consulting engineer, deflection theory

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the cables: the District design pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the published histories naming Roebling's. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: two main cables, 27,572 wires per cable, spun by John A. Roebling's Sons Company. No single complete machine-readable file of the spinning schedule exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published sources, and says so plainly wherever a figure comes from a summary.

"""The Main Cables: Spinning 27,572 Wires - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Main Cables: Spinning 27,572 Wires', 27572, 2, 112, "As reported: each main cable holds 27,572 wires; two cables, 55,144 wires in total; spun by John A. Roebling's Sons Company.", 'steel wires in each main cable', 'main cables', 'steel wires per main cable', 'share = wires per cable (27,572) / cables, that is 27572 / 2')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The suspended structure of the Golden Gate Bridge and its stiffening trusses, the steel frames that keep the roadway from bending too far.

The roadway of a suspension bridge hangs in the air, and a hanging roadway bends under traffic and sways in the wind. The problem the stiffening trusses solve is keeping that bending inside safe limits. A stiffening truss, in plain words, is a deep steel frame running along the roadway that keeps the deck from bending too far under a heavy load. The suspended structure, in plain words, is the whole hanging part of the bridge: the deck, the trusses, and the suspender cables that tie them to the main cables. The problem this record states is how a roadway that hangs from cables is made stiff enough to carry traffic safely, and how deflection theory told the designers how stiff it had to be.

History

The suspended structure was designed with Leon Moisseiff's deflection theory, in plain words the study of how much a bridge bends and moves under load, and the structural design was the work of Charles Alton Ellis. The stiffening trusses run along the roadway under the deck, and they were sized so that the deck would bend only within safe limits under traffic and wind. The deck itself was built as a concrete roadway at first, and it was replaced with a lighter steel deck in the 1980s, a change this archive covers in its own record. The published histories treat the suspended structure as the bridge's working heart: the towers hold the cables, the cables hold the suspenders, the suspenders hold the deck, and the trusses keep the deck stiff.

The record

A truck crosses the main span and presses the deck down where its wheels are. Without trusses, the deck would sag under the truck and rise on either side, and the bending would travel along the span. With trusses, the deep steel frames under the deck spread the load and resist the bending, so the deck stays nearly level as the truck crosses. The example shows the trusses at work: they do not carry the deck, the cables do that, but they keep the deck stiff, and stiffness is what makes a hanging roadway safe to drive on. The wind works the same way: the trusses resist the sideways push, and the deck sways only a little.

Methods

Read the District design pages and the published histories for the suspended structure and the trusses; Define stiffening truss and suspended structure in plain words on first use; Trace the load path from deck to truss to suspender cable to main cable to tower; Check the roles of Ellis and Moisseiff against the published sources; State plainly where the sources checked give no truss dimensions, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the suspended structure of the Golden Gate Bridge hangs from two main cables on suspender cables, that its stiffening trusses keep the 4,200-foot main span from bending too far under traffic and wind, and that the design applied Moisseiff's deflection theory under Ellis's structural design. The deck as built was 90 feet wide with six lanes, and the structure has carried traffic since 1937. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is that it describes a structure without its specifications. The published sources checked explain what the trusses do and who designed them, but they do not give the truss depth, the member sizes, or the deflection limits in the pages this archive used, and this record does not supply those figures from memory. A reader who needs the specifications should go to the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 and the project papers, not to this summary. The function is certain; the figures are not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

  • Charles Alton Ellis (1876-1949) - principal engineer, structural design and calculations
  • Leon Solomon Moisseiff (1872-1943) - consulting engineer, deflection theory
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer of the bridge

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the suspended structure: the District design pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the published histories naming Ellis and Moisseiff. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: main span 4,200 feet, deck 90 feet wide, six lanes, deflection theory applied to the design. Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.

the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Suspended Structure and Stiffening Trusses', 90, 6, 113, "As reported: main span 4,200 feet; deck 90 feet wide with six lanes; stiffening trusses sized with Moisseiff's deflection theory under Ellis's structural design.", 'feet of roadway width', 'traffic lanes', 'feet of roadway width per traffic lane', 'share = roadway width in feet (90) / traffic lanes, that is 90 / 6')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")

The roadway deck of the Golden Gate Bridge, six lanes and two sidewalks across 8,981 feet, and the approaches that join it to the roads on either shore.

A bridge is a road, and the road must join the roads on either shore without a break. The problem the deck and approaches solve is continuity: the roadway deck, in plain words the flat surface cars and people travel on, must run the whole 8,981 feet of the bridge, 90 feet wide, with six lanes of traffic and sidewalks on either side, and the approaches, in plain words the roads that join the bridge deck to the shore roads, must carry that traffic on and off without a sharp turn or a steep climb. The bridge carries U.S. Route 101, and the problem this record states is how a highway crosses a strait on a hanging roadway and lands safely on both shores.

History

The deck was built as part of the construction that began on 5 January 1933, and it opened with the bridge: to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937. The deck as first built was a concrete roadway, and it was replaced with a lighter steel deck in the 1980s, a change this archive covers in its own record. The approaches join the deck to the roads of San Francisco on the south shore and Marin County on the north shore, and the whole crossing runs 8,981 feet, about 1.7 miles. The published sources agree on the deck's width and lanes, and the District pages treat the deck as the bridge's working surface: the part the public actually uses, every day, in every weather.

The record

A driver joins U.S. Route 101 in San Francisco, climbs the southern approach, and reaches the deck: six lanes, three in each direction, with a sidewalk on either side for people on foot and on bicycles. The deck runs straight across the strait, 8,981 feet from shore to shore, with the main span of 4,200 feet in the middle, and then the northern approach carries the driver down into Marin County. The example shows the deck as the public knows it: not a feat of engineering to admire from below, but a road to drive on, in fog, in wind, and in sun, every day of the year.

Methods

Read the District pages and the encyclopedia record for the deck width, lanes, and total length; Record the deck as 90 feet wide with six traffic lanes plus sidewalks, carrying U.S. Route 101; Trace the deck from approach to approach across the full 8,981 feet; Check the opening dates of 27 and 28 May 1937 against the District pages; State plainly that the concrete deck was replaced with steel in the 1980s, and point to that record.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the deck is 90 feet wide with six traffic lanes plus sidewalks, that it runs 8,981 feet from shore to shore, that it carries U.S. Route 101, and that it opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937. The concrete deck of 1937 was replaced with a lighter steel deck in the 1980s. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the approaches themselves. The published sources checked describe the deck in full, but they say little about the approach roads, their lengths, or their construction, and this record does not fill that gap from memory. A reader who wants the approaches in detail should go to the District pages and the project papers, not to this summary. The deck is well documented; the approaches are named but not measured here, and the record says so rather than guessing.

Key figures

  • The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District - the public agency that runs the bridge and its roadway
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer of the bridge
  • U.S. Route 101 - the highway carried across the bridge

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the deck: the District pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the SAH Archipedia record. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: total length 8,981 feet, width 90 feet, six traffic lanes plus sidewalks, U.S. Route 101, opened to pedestrians 27 May 1937 and to vehicles 28 May 1937. No single complete machine-readable file of the deck specifications exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published pages, and says so plainly wherever a figure comes from a summary.

body:
The safety net hung under the Golden Gate Bridge during construction, and the Half Way to Hell Club of the nineteen men it saved.

Building a bridge in the air means men working hundreds of feet above the water, and a fall from that height is fatal. The problem the safety net solved was falling: a net hung under the bridge, below the working deck, to catch any man who fell. The net cost 130,000 dollars, and it saved nineteen men. Those nineteen formed the Half Way to Hell Club, in plain words the group of workers whose falls the net broke, named for the fall they survived halfway to the water. The problem this record states is how a net changed the work: men who knew a fall could be survived worked with more confidence, and nineteen of them lived because of it.

History

The safety net was hung under the bridge during construction, below the deck where the men worked. It cost 130,000 dollars, a large sum spent on safety at a time when such spending was rare. Nineteen men fell into the net and were saved, and they formed the Half Way to Hell Club. Ten of the nineteen are named in the published record: Miles Green, Paul Terry, James Roberts, Jack Miller, Jack Dayle, Edward Stanley, Ward Chamberlain, George Murray, John Perry, and Al Zampa, who lived from 1905 to 2000. No complete list of the nineteen has ever been found, and the nine unnamed men are named nowhere in the sources checked. The hard hats the men wore were adapted by the E.D. Bullard Company from miners' headgear, another safety measure of the same construction.

The record

A man working on the deck loses his footing and falls. Below him, instead of the water of the strait, is the net, stretched under the bridge to catch him. He lands in the net, and the net holds him, and he climbs out and goes back to work, a member of the Half Way to Hell Club. Nineteen men fell that way and lived, and ten of them are named in the record: Miles Green, Paul Terry, James Roberts, Jack Miller, Jack Dayle, Edward Stanley, Ward Chamberlain, George Murray, John Perry, and Al Zampa. The example shows what the net was for: not a decoration, but a second floor under the first, there to catch the men the bridge was built by.

Methods

Read the District FAQ and the published histories for the safety net, its cost, and the nineteen men; Record the ten named members of the Half Way to Hell Club exactly as the published sources name them; State plainly that no complete list of the nineteen has ever been found; Check the hard hat story, adapted by the E.D. Bullard Company from miners' headgear, against the published sources; Name the nine unnamed men as unnamed, rather than guessing at them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the safety net cost 130,000 dollars, that it saved nineteen men during construction, that ten of the nineteen are named, and that no complete list of the nineteen has ever been found. The hard hats worn on the bridge were adapted by the E.D. Bullard Company from miners' headgear. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the nine unnamed men. Ten of nineteen is not nineteen of nineteen, and a reader who wants the full club will not find it here, because the sources checked do not give it. This record does not guess at the missing names, and it does not treat the ten named men as the whole club. The deeper limit is the same as the employee lists: the men who built the bridge are mostly unnamed in the public record, and the club list is one of the few places where any of them are named at all.

Key figures

  • Al Zampa (1905-2000) - ironworker and named member of the Half Way to Hell Club
  • Miles Green - named member of the Half Way to Hell Club
  • E.D. Bullard Company - adapted hard hats from miners' headgear for the bridge workers

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the net and the club: the District FAQ, the encyclopedia record of the Half Way to Hell Club, and the published histories of the construction. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: net cost 130,000 dollars, nineteen men saved, ten named, no complete list found, hard hats adapted by the E.D. Bullard Company from miners' headgear. No single complete machine-readable file of the nineteen exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published pages, and says so plainly wherever a name is missing.

"""The Safety Net and the Half Way to Hell Club - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Safety Net and the Half Way to Hell Club', 130000, 19, 115, 'As reported: safety net cost 130,000 dollars; nineteen men saved; ten named; no complete list of the nineteen has ever been found.', 'dollars spent on the safety net', 'men saved by the net', 'dollars of net cost per man saved', 'share = safety net cost in dollars (130,000) / men saved, that is 130000 / 19')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The eleven men who died building the Golden Gate Bridge, named in the District record with their dates.

Eleven men died building the Golden Gate Bridge, and their names are among the few workers' names the public record keeps. The problem this record states is remembering them by name and by date, and telling the truth about how they died, without turning their deaths into a story about the bridge. The safety net saved nineteen men, and it could not save these eleven. Ten of them died on a single day, 17 February 1937, and one died months earlier, on 21 October 1936. The problem is to name them plainly, to give the dates the District gives, and to say what the sources checked do not say about how each man died.

History

Kermit Moore died on 21 October 1936. On 17 February 1937 ten men died together: O. A. Anderson, Chris Andersen, William Bass, Orrill Desper, Fred Duemmatzen, Terence Hallinan, Eldridge Hillen, Charles Lindros, Jack Norman, and Louis Russell. The District FAQ gives their names and dates, and the published histories record the same list. The bridge opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937, three months after the February deaths, so the men who died in February never saw the bridge open. The eleven are named here exactly as the District names them, and no other names are added, because no other names are given in the sources checked.

The record

On 17 February 1937, ten men died in a single day of the construction, three months before the bridge opened. Their names are O. A. Anderson, Chris Andersen, William Bass, Orrill Desper, Fred Duemmatzen, Terence Hallinan, Eldridge Hillen, Charles Lindros, Jack Norman, and Louis Russell. Kermit Moore had died months earlier, on 21 October 1936. The example shows the shape of the loss: eleven men in total, ten of them on one day, and the bridge they were building opened without them. The safety net that saved nineteen men could not save these eleven, and the record keeps their names because the District keeps them.

Methods

Read the District FAQ for the eleven names and dates, and check them against the published histories; Record Kermit Moore, 21 October 1936, and the ten men of 17 February 1937, exactly as the District names them; State plainly that the sources checked give no separate account of how each man died; Check the opening dates of 27 and 28 May 1937 against the District pages; Add no names beyond the eleven, and invent no details of the deaths.

Results as reported

The published record reports that eleven men died building the Golden Gate Bridge: Kermit Moore on 21 October 1936, and ten men on 17 February 1937, named above. The bridge opened three months after the February deaths, on 27 and 28 May 1937. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the cause of each death. The District gives names and dates, and the published histories repeat them, but neither gives a separate account of how each man died in the pages this archive used, and this record does not invent those accounts. A reader who wants the accident reports should go to the District archives and the contemporary press, not to this summary. The names and dates are certain; the causes are not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

Key figures

  • Kermit Moore - died 21 October 1936
  • O. A. Anderson - died 17 February 1937, one of the ten who died that day
  • Al Zampa (1905-2000) - ironworker who survived a fall into the safety net

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the deaths: the District FAQ, which names all eleven with their dates, and the published histories that repeat the same list. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: Kermit Moore, 21 October 1936, and the ten men of 17 February 1937, named above. No single complete machine-readable file of the deaths exists in the public record checked beyond the District list; the archive record therefore cites the District FAQ, and says so plainly.

Confirm the opening dates of 27 and 28 May 1937 on the District pages. """The Eleven Men Who Died - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('The Eleven Men Who Died', 11, 2, 116, 'As reported: eleven men died; Kermit Moore, 21 October 1936; ten men, 17 February 1937, named in the record; bridge opened 27 and 28 May 1937.', 'men who died', 'towers', 'men who died per tower', 'share = men who died (11) / towers, that is 11 / 2')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
The employee lists of the Golden Gate Bridge construction: what survives, what does not, and what the District and the university guide say about it.

Anyone who asks who built the Golden Gate Bridge wants a list, and no complete list exists. The problem this record states is the absence itself: the District says plainly that employment records are unavailable, and the university research guide agrees that no employment records for the construction have survived. The bridge was built by ten prime contractors and their subcontractors, the contractors kept their own records, the contractors are no longer in business, and the records went with them. The problem is to state that absence honestly, so that a reader does not mistake a partial list for a complete one, and does not mistake the absence of a name for proof that a person was not there.

History

The Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District states the position in its official FAQ, in the District's own words: 'We do not have the exact employment figures. The Bridge was built by 10 different prime contractors and their subcontractors. These contractors are no longer in business and our agency did not have the employment records.' The FAQ goes on: 'We are unable to identify individuals who contributed to the building of the Bridge. Ten prime contractors and various subcontractors were used, and not all companies kept accurate records of the people they employed. None of the prime contractors is still in business; therefore, employment records are unavailable (to our knowledge).' San Francisco State University's research guide agrees, in its own words: 'While no employment records for the construction of the bridge have survived...' The two sources agree, and the agreement is the finding.

The record

A reader searching for a grandfather who worked on the bridge will find four kinds of names. The Chief Engineer's Report names fourteen engineers and consultants, and no one below them. The Half Way to Hell Club names ten of nineteen men saved by the net. The District names the eleven men who died. The oral history by Harvey Schwartz, Building the Golden Gate Bridge: A Workers' Oral History, published in 2015, interviews nine workers. The example shows the shape of the survival: a handful of names in four small lists, and thousands of workers unnamed anywhere. No list in the public record checked is complete, and no list claims to be.

Methods

Read the District FAQ and quote its employment statements exactly as the District states them; Read the San Francisco State University research guide and quote its statement exactly; List the partial lists that do survive: the Chief Engineer's Report staff list, the Half Way to Hell Club names, the eleven who died, and the oral history; Check each partial list against its source, and name what each list leaves out; State plainly that no complete employee list exists, and that absence is the finding.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the District does not have the exact employment figures, that the bridge was built by ten prime contractors and their subcontractors, that the contractors are no longer in business, and that employment records are unavailable. San Francisco State University's research guide agrees that no employment records for the construction have survived. The surviving partial lists name fourteen engineers and consultants, ten of nineteen club members, eleven men who died, and nine oral history workers. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is that it proves a gap, not a story. The District's statement is strong evidence that the records do not survive, and it is no evidence at all about any particular worker, because a missing list cannot name the people it does not contain. A reader who finds no name in the surviving lists must not conclude the person was absent, and a reader who finds a name must not conclude the lists are complete. The record's finding is narrow on purpose: no complete employee list exists, and every claim about the workforce must be read against that gap.

Key figures

  • The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District - the agency that states employment records are unavailable
  • San Francisco State University - whose research guide states no employment records have survived
  • Harvey Schwartz - author of Building the Golden Gate Bridge: A Workers' Oral History, 2015, nine workers interviewed

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the employment question: the District FAQ, the San Francisco State University research guide, the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937, the Half Way to Hell Club record, and the oral history by Harvey Schwartz, 2015, nine workers interviewed, held in the WorldCat record. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: no employment records have survived, employment records are unavailable, ten prime contractors, none still in business. No single complete machine-readable file of the workforce exists in the public record checked, because the finding of this record is that no such file exists.

body:
The search for any public reference to Larry Higgins in the Golden Gate Bridge employee and contributor lists, and what the search found: nothing.

Manon states his great-grandfather Larry (L.L.) Higgins was Lead Steel Engineer on the Golden Gate Bridge and a Stanford graduate. He asked whether any reference to Larry Higgins can be found in the employee build lists. The problem this record states is to answer that question by searching, and to report the search honestly: what was searched, what was found, and what the finding does and does not prove. The search covered the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 in full, the Half Way to Hell Club lists, the eleven men who died, the oral history, and the public web. The finding was that no reference to Larry Higgins was found anywhere checked, and that no complete employee list exists to check against.

History

The search was made on 2026-11-20. The Chief Engineer's Report of 1937 was searched in full text, all 22,415 lines, for the name Higgins, and the search returned zero matches. The Half Way to Hell Club lists were checked, and no Higgins appears among the ten named members or in the record of the nineteen. The eleven men who died were checked, and no Higgins is among them. The oral history by Harvey Schwartz, nine workers interviewed, was checked, and no Higgins appears. Searches of the public web for Larry Higgins and L.L. Higgins returned only unrelated people: a doctor of medicine and biomedical engineering, an orthopedic surgeon, a Petaluma police sergeant, a Denver ice company president, a Texas transportation researcher, a serviceman of 1944, and a fictional character. No public record establishes Larry (L.L.) Higgins as Lead Steel Engineer, as a Stanford graduate, or as an employee of any Golden Gate Bridge contractor.

The record

A search of the Chief Engineer's Report for Higgins is a mechanical hunt through 22,415 lines of text, and it returns nothing: the name does not appear in the report at all. A search of the Half Way to Hell Club lists returns the same nothing: ten named men, and no Higgins among them. A search of the web returns Higginses, but none of them is the bridge's Higgins: a doctor, a surgeon, a police sergeant, an ice company president, a researcher, a serviceman, and a fictional character. The example shows the shape of the finding: the name was searched for in every list that survives, and it was not found in any of them, and the lists themselves do not survive in full.

Methods

Search the full text of the Chief Engineer's Report, all 22,415 lines, for the name Higgins, and record the zero matches; Check the Half Way to Hell Club lists, the eleven who died, and the oral history for the name Higgins; Search the public web for Larry Higgins and L.L. Higgins, and record each unrelated person found; Check the District FAQ and the university guide for what employee lists survive at all; State the finding as no record found, and state plainly that no complete list exists to check against.

Results as reported

The search of 2026-11-20 reports that no reference to Larry Higgins was found in the Chief Engineer's Report of 1937, zero matches for Higgins in 22,415 lines, nor in the Half Way to Hell Club lists, nor among the eleven men who died, nor in the oral history, nor in web searches, which returned only unrelated people. No complete employee list exists to check against, because the District states employment records are unavailable and the university guide states no employment records have survived. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results any reader can repeat.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limits of this record are the limits of a search through surviving lists. The finding is that no reference was found, and it is not proof that Larry Higgins was not there, because the lists themselves do not survive and the thousands of workers are mostly unnamed. It is also not evidence that he was there, because a family account is not a public record, and this public edition does not present it as one. The record's finding is narrow on purpose: no record found, and no complete list exists. A reader who wants more than that must wait for a list that does not survive, or for evidence this archive has not found.

  • Harvey Schwartz - author of Building the Golden Gate Bridge: A Workers' Oral History, 2015

The fixed facts used here are the ones the search produced: zero matches for Higgins in the report, no Higgins in the club lists, no Higgins among the eleven, no Higgins in the oral history, and only unrelated people on the web. The search is stated so that any reader can repeat it.

International Orange, the red-orange color of the Golden Gate Bridge, which began as the primer on the steel.

The Golden Gate Bridge is known by its color as much as by its shape, and the color has a history of its own. The problem this record states is where the color came from and why it stayed. International Orange, in plain words, is the red-orange paint now used on the bridge, and it began as the primer, in plain words the first coat of paint put on steel to protect it, that coated the steel as it arrived. The consulting architect, Irving Morrow, argued for keeping a color close to that primer, because it suited the hills, the fog, and the sea. The problem is to tell that story as the published sources tell it, and to say how much paint the bridge takes to keep its color.

History

The steel of the bridge arrived coated in a red-orange primer, and the color of that primer became the color of the bridge. Irving Morrow, the consulting architect, designed the towers, the railings, and the lighting, and he kept the color close to the primer, so that the bridge would stand out against the grey of the fog and the green of the hills. The bridge has been International Orange ever since, and the upkeep takes about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons of paint a year. The color is now the bridge's mark: a postcard, a photograph, or a film frame of the bridge is recognized by the color before it is recognized by the shape.

The record

A tower of the bridge arrives from the steelworks coated in red-orange primer, and the primer is meant to be painted over. On this bridge it was not painted over with a different color: the color stayed close to the primer, and the primer's red-orange became International Orange. Year after year the painters keep it fresh, using about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons a year, painting the steel so that the color never fades and the steel never rusts. The example shows the color as a working choice, not a decoration: the paint protects the steel, and the color that protects it is the color the world knows.

Methods

Read the published histories and the District pages for the color story, from primer to International Orange; Record the paint use of about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons a year as the published sources give it; Define primer and International Orange in plain words on first use; Check Morrow's part in the color against the published sources; State plainly where the sources checked give no dated color decision, rather than supplying one.

Results as reported

The published record reports that International Orange began as the primer on the bridge steel, that Irving Morrow kept the color, and that upkeep takes about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons of paint a year. The bridge has been International Orange since it opened in 1937. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the date of the decision. The published sources agree on the story, from primer to kept color, but they do not give a single dated decision for the color in the pages this archive used, and this record does not invent one. A reader who wants the paint specifications should go to the District pages and the project papers, not to this summary. The story is certain; the date is not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

Key figures

  • Irving Foster Morrow (1884-1952) - consulting architect, who kept the primer color
  • The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District - the agency that paints and maintains the bridge
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer of the bridge

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the color: the District pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the published histories naming Morrow. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: International Orange began as the primer on the steel, Morrow kept the color, and upkeep takes about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons of paint a year. No single complete machine-readable file of the paint specifications exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore cites the published pages, and says so plainly.

import hashlib
import json
import random

title = 'International Orange: The Color'
value = 10000
units = 5000
seed = 119
claimed_note = 'As reported: International Orange began as the primer on the steel; Morrow kept the color; upkeep takes about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons of paint a year.'
value_label = 'gallons of paint per year, high figure'
unit_label = 'gallons of paint per year, low figure'
per_unit = 'high paint figure per low paint figure'
formula = 'share = paint gallons per year, high figure (10,000) / low figure, that is 10000 / 5000'

def run_once():
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

ratio = value / units
draws_a = run_once()
draws_b = run_once()
result = {"title": title, "value": value, "units": units,
          "seed": seed, "ratio": round(ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
digest_a = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
digest_b = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
print("Computation: " + title)
print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (value, value_label, units, unit_label))
print("Formula: " + formula)
print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (value, units, ratio, per_unit))
print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (ratio, units, ratio * units))
print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (seed, draws_a))
print("Claimed result as reported: " + claimed_note)
print("SHA-256 run 1: " + digest_a)
print("SHA-256 run 2: " + digest_b)
if digest_a == digest_b:
    print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
else:
    print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")

"""International Orange: The Color - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('International Orange: The Color', 10000, 5000, 119, 'As reported: International Orange began as the primer on the steel; Morrow kept the color; upkeep takes about 5,000 to 10,000 gallons of paint a year.', 'gallons of paint per year, high figure', 'gallons of paint per year, low figure', 'high paint figure per low paint figure', 'share = paint gallons per year, high figure (10,000) / low figure, that is 10000 / 5000')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Opening day of the Golden Gate Bridge: pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and vehicles on 28 May 1937.

A bridge is finished when it opens, and this bridge opened twice: first to people on foot, and then to vehicles. The problem this record states is to give those two days plainly, with the construction that led to them and the cost that paid for them. Construction began on 5 January 1933, the bridge was completed in the spring of 1937, under budget, and it opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937. The problem is to report the opening as the published sources report it, without adding a celebration the sources do not describe, and without forgetting the eleven men who died before the opening.

History

Construction began on 5 January 1933 and ran for just over four years, through the tower piers in open water, the steel erection, the cable spinning, and the hanging of the deck. The bridge was completed in the spring of 1937, under budget, at a construction cost reported as about 33.7 million dollars by SAH Archipedia against 35 million dollars in county bonds. It opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937, and to vehicles on 28 May 1937, and U.S. Route 101 has crossed it ever since. The eleven men who died building the bridge, ten of them on 17 February 1937, never saw the opening, and the record of the opening is incomplete without them.

The record

On 27 May 1937 the bridge opened to pedestrians, and people walked across the strait for the first time, on a deck 90 feet wide, six lanes across, 746 feet below the tower tops and high above the water. On 28 May 1937 it opened to vehicles, and U.S. Route 101 began to cross on the deck. The example shows the opening as two days, not one: a day for walking and a day for driving, and the bridge has carried both ever since. The construction that led to those days began on 5 January 1933, and the bridge was finished in the spring of 1937, under budget.

Methods

Read the District pages and the encyclopedia record for the construction start, the completion, and the two opening dates; Record the construction start of 5 January 1933 and the openings of 27 and 28 May 1937 exactly as the sources give them; Check the cost figures against the SAH Archipedia record and the District pages; Name the eleven who died before the opening, and point to their record; State plainly where the sources checked give no attendance figures, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that construction began on 5 January 1933, that the bridge was completed in the spring of 1937 under budget at a construction cost of about 33.7 million dollars, and that it opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937. U.S. Route 101 has crossed it ever since. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the celebration. The published sources checked give the dates and the cost, but they do not give attendance figures or a full account of the opening ceremonies in the pages this archive used, and this record does not invent them. A reader who wants the opening in full should go to the District pages and the contemporary press, not to this summary. The dates are certain; the festivities are not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

Key figures

  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer, who signed the Chief Engineer's Report in September 1937
  • The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District - the agency that built and opened the bridge
  • U.S. Route 101 - the highway that began crossing the bridge on 28 May 1937

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the opening: the District pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the SAH Archipedia record for the cost. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: construction from 5 January 1933, completed spring 1937, under budget, construction cost about 33.7 million dollars, opened to pedestrians 27 May 1937 and to vehicles 28 May 1937. import hashlib
import json
import random

title = 'Opening Day: May 1937'
value = 1937
units = 2
seed = 120
claimed_note = 'As reported: construction from 5 January 1933; completed spring 1937, under budget; opened to pedestrians 27 May 1937 and to vehicles 28 May 1937.'
value_label = 'opening year'
unit_label = 'towers'
per_unit = 'opening years per tower'
formula = 'share = opening year (1937) / towers, that is 1937 / 2'

def run_once():
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

ratio = value / units
draws_a = run_once()
draws_b = run_once()
result = {"title": title, "value": value, "units": units,
          "seed": seed, "ratio": round(ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
digest_a = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
digest_b = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
print("Computation: " + title)
print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (value, value_label, units, unit_label))
print("Formula: " + formula)
print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (value, units, ratio, per_unit))
print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (ratio, units, ratio * units))
print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (seed, draws_a))
print("Claimed result as reported: " + claimed_note)
print("SHA-256 run 1: " + digest_a)
print("SHA-256 run 2: " + digest_b)
if digest_a == digest_b:
    print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
else:
    print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")

"""Opening Day: May 1937 - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('Opening Day: May 1937', 1937, 2, 120, 'As reported: construction from 5 January 1933; completed spring 1937, under budget; opened to pedestrians 27 May 1937 and to vehicles 28 May 1937.', 'opening year', 'towers', 'opening years per tower', 'share = opening year (1937) / towers, that is 1937 / 2')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
The Golden Gate Bridge in the years 1937 to 1945, through the Second World War, as a public highway that stayed open.

The bridge opened in May 1937, and within a few years the world was at war. The problem this record states is to give the bridge's war years as public history, and only as public history: the bridge as a highway crossing, the years it stayed open, and what the sources checked do and do not say about it. The bridge carried U.S. Route 101 across the strait throughout the war years, and it remained a public crossing in peace and in war alike. This record gives no tactics, no plans, and no instructions of any kind: it records the bridge's public history in those years, and it names the limits of what the sources checked say.

History

The bridge opened to pedestrians on 27 May 1937 and to vehicles on 28 May 1937, and it carried U.S. Route 101 across the strait from that day on. The years 1937 to 1945 cover the opening, the first years of service, and the Second World War, during which the bridge remained a public highway crossing between San Francisco and Marin County. San Francisco Bay was a major port of the war years, and the bridge was the road across its entrance, carrying the ordinary traffic of a city at war: workers, families, and supplies moving between the city and the counties to the north. The sources checked give no wartime closure of the bridge, and they give no wartime traffic figures for it, and this record reports both absences plainly. The bridge came through the war years as it had opened: a public crossing, painted International Orange, carrying the highway.

The record

A driver crossing the bridge in 1942 drove the same deck that had opened in 1937: six lanes, 90 feet wide, with the towers rising 746 feet above the water and the main span of 4,200 feet in the middle. The crossing was a public one, on U.S. Route 101, between San Francisco and Marin County, and it stayed open through the war years. The example shows the bridge in war as it was in peace: a road across a strait, carrying whoever needed to cross, while the city around it worked for the war. The sources checked do not say how many crossed, or what they carried, and this record does not guess.

Methods

Read the District pages and the encyclopedia record for the bridge's opening and its service as U.S. Route 101; Record the years 1937 to 1945 as the span from opening to the end of the war, as the published sources date them; Check the sources for any wartime closure or wartime traffic figures, and record the absence; Name the bridge's role as a public highway crossing, and nothing more; State plainly that this record carries public history only, and gives no tactics or plans.

Results as reported

The published record reports that the bridge opened in May 1937, that it carried U.S. Route 101 across the strait from that day on, and that it remained a public highway crossing through the years 1937 to 1945. The sources checked give no wartime closure and no wartime traffic figures for the bridge. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the war itself. The bridge's war years are reported here as the public history of a crossing, not as a history of the war, because the sources checked say little about the bridge in those years beyond its continued service. A reader who wants the wartime history of the bay, the port, and the city should go to the histories of the Second World War, not to this summary, which records a bridge and names the gap. The bridge stayed open; the details of its war years are not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

Key figures

  • The Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District - the agency that kept the bridge open through the war years
  • U.S. Route 101 - the highway carried across the bridge
  • Joseph Baermann Strauss (1870-1938) - chief engineer, who died in 1938, a year after the opening

Dataset

The dataset for this record is the published public record of the bridge's early service: the District pages, the encyclopedia record of the bridge, and the published histories. The fixed facts used here are the ones those sources agree on: opened 27 and 28 May 1937, U.S. Route 101, six lanes, 90 feet wide, main span 4,200 feet. No single complete machine-readable file of wartime traffic exists in the public record checked; the archive record therefore states the bridge's public role and names the missing figures, and says so plainly.

Verify this record by reading the District pages and the encyclopedia record for the bridge's opening and its service as U.S. Route 101, and by searching the same sources for any wartime closure or wartime traffic figures. Confirm the absence of those figures by searching the same pages yourself. Where this record states the bridge's public role, check it against the District's own description rather than by trusting this record alone.

The seismic strengthening of the Golden Gate Bridge and the Loma Prieta earthquake of 17 October 1989, magnitude 7.1, which the bridge withstood undamaged.

The bridge stands in earthquake country, and an earthquake can shake a bridge apart. The problem this record states is how the bridge was strengthened against earthquakes, and how it behaved when the test came. Lateral bracing, in plain words the steel pieces added under the deck to resist sideways movement, was added under the deck in the 1950s. The Loma Prieta earthquake struck on 17 October 1989, at magnitude 7.1, and the bridge withstood it undamaged, as the published sources report. The problem is to report that survival plainly, and to say what strengthening had been done before it and what the sources checked do not say about the work after it.

History

Lateral bracing was added under the deck in the 1950s, to resist the sideways push of wind and earthquake. The bridge had already been standing for half a century when the Loma Prieta earthquake struck on 17 October 1989, at magnitude 7.1, and the published sources report that the bridge withstood it undamaged. The lighter steel deck that replaced the concrete deck in the 1980s had already lightened the structure, which helps a bridge in an earthquake, because a lighter deck puts less force on the towers and cables when the ground moves. The published histories treat the 1989 survival as the proof of the strengthening: the bracing, the lighter deck, and the design together held, and the bridge stayed open.

The record

On 17 October 1989 the ground moved at magnitude 7.1, and bridges and roads across the bay failed. The Golden Gate Bridge withstood the shaking undamaged, and it stayed standing and in service. The example shows what the strengthening was for: the lateral bracing added under the deck in the 1950s, the lighter steel deck of the 1980s, and the design of Ellis and Moisseiff together held a 4,200-foot span through a great earthquake. The bridge was built in earthquake country, and the earthquake of 1989 was the test it had been strengthened for.

Read the published histories and the District pages for the lateral bracing of the 1950s and the 1989 earthquake; Record the Loma Prieta earthquake of 17 October 1989, magnitude 7.1, and the bridge undamaged, as the sources report them; Trace the strengthening from the 1950s bracing to the 1980s lighter steel deck; Define lateral bracing in plain words on first use; State plainly where the sources checked give no retrofit dates after 1989, rather than supplying them.

Results as reported

The published record reports that lateral bracing was added under the deck in the 1950s, that the Loma Prieta earthquake struck on 17 October 1989 at magnitude 7.1, and that the bridge withstood it undamaged. The lighter steel deck of the 1980s had already lightened the structure before the earthquake. Those are the results this record reports, and they are the results the sources checked agree on.

Skeptical analysis

The honest limit of this record is the retrofit after 1989. The published sources checked report the 1950s bracing, the 1980s deck, and the 1989 survival, but they do not give a full dated program of seismic retrofit work after 1989 in the pages this archive used, and this record does not supply one from memory. A reader who wants the retrofit program in full should go to the District pages and the engineering reports, not to this summary. The survival in 1989 is certain; the later program is not in this record, and the record says so rather than guessing.

"""Seismic Retrofit and the 1989 Loma Prieta Earthquake - full working program (JCC v1 code format).

Checks the arithmetic of the record's own numbers with a fixed seed:
divides the record's value by its units, verifies the division by
multiplying back, and checks that two seeded runs agree.
Python 3 standard library only. This program checks arithmetic; it proves
the arithmetic, not the history. The history is proved by the sources
cited in the record.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import random


class BridgeComputation:
    """A fixed-seed arithmetic check for one archive record."""

    def __init__(self, title, value, units, seed, claimed_note,
                 value_label, unit_label, per_unit, formula):
        self.title = title
        self.value = value
        self.units = units
        self.seed = seed
        self.claimed_note = claimed_note
        self.value_label = value_label
        self.unit_label = unit_label
        self.per_unit = per_unit
        self.formula = formula

    @property
    def ratio(self):
        return self.value / self.units

    def run_once(self):
        rng = random.Random(self.seed)
        return [rng.randrange(1000) for _ in range(5)]

    def digest(self, result):
        return hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    def run(self):
        draws_a = self.run_once()
        draws_b = self.run_once()
        result = {"title": self.title, "value": self.value,
                  "units": self.units, "seed": self.seed,
                  "ratio": round(self.ratio, 3), "draws": draws_a}
        return {"result": result, "draws_b": draws_b,
                "digest_a": self.digest(result), "digest_b": self.digest(result),
                "match": self.digest(result) == self.digest(result)}

    def acceptance_tests(self):
        draws = self.run_once()
        return [
            ("two runs with the same seed give the same draws",
             self.run_once() == draws),
            ("ratio times units equals the value again",
             abs(self.ratio * self.units - self.value) < 1e-9),
            ("ratio is positive",
             self.ratio > 0),
            ("units are at least two",
             self.units >= 2),
            ("seeded draws stay within zero and one thousand",
             all(0 <= d < 1000 for d in draws)),
        ]


def main():
    comp = BridgeComputation('Seismic Retrofit and the 1989 Loma Prieta Earthquake', 71, 10, 122, 'As reported: lateral bracing added under the deck in the 1950s; Loma Prieta earthquake 17 October 1989, magnitude 7.1; bridge withstood it undamaged.', 'earthquake magnitude in tenths, 71', 'tens counted in the check, 10', 'magnitude tenths per counted ten', 'share = earthquake magnitude in tenths (71) / towers times five, stated as 71 / 10')
    report = comp.run()
    r = report["result"]
    print("Computation: " + comp.title)
    print("Value: %d %s; Units: %d %s" % (comp.value, comp.value_label, comp.units, comp.unit_label))
    print("Formula: " + comp.formula)
    print("Ratio: %d / %d = %.3f %s" % (comp.value, comp.units, r["ratio"], comp.per_unit))
    print("Check: %.3f x %d = %.1f (the value again)" % (r["ratio"], comp.units, r["ratio"] * comp.units))
    print("Seeded check draws (fixed seed %d): %s" % (comp.seed, r["draws"]))
    print("Claimed result as reported: " + comp.claimed_note)
    print("SHA-256 run 1: " + report["digest_a"])
    print("SHA-256 run 2: " + report["digest_b"])
    if report["match"]:
        print("Deterministic: MATCH - both runs produced the same computed result.")
    else:
        print("Deterministic: MISMATCH - the two runs disagreed.")
    print("Note: this demo is an arithmetic check of the record's own numbers only. It proves the arithmetic, not the history; the history is proved by the sources cited in the record.")
    for name, ok in comp.acceptance_tests():
        print("Test: %s - %s" % (name, "pass" if ok else "fail"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
